blocks.p: Rei found the ninth seat the way sailors find weather. By where the city bent round it.

Higuchi's note gave no address, because there was no address. Gin's file said the only safe way to reach the Hunger holder was through the Grid's emergency protocols, and Rei had no one in the Grid to ask that night. So he used what Higuchi had given him instead. Not an address but a habit. A route that was never the same route twice. And a single line in Higuchi's cramped hand.
He eats so he does not have to stop, and he moves so the appetite cannot find the door.

So Rei walked Ueno after dark in the second week of Obon. The air was thick with grilling fat and incense and the sweet burnt smell of taiyaki. Lanterns swung over the food stalls. Under the railway the crowds moved in slow warm currents, and the sound of the trains overhead came down through the steel like weather. He passed the all-night ramen counters and the conveyor-belt sushi places still lit at one in the morning. He looked not for a face but for a kind of motion. Somewhere between the station and the park he began to feel it, the way he had felt the cold on the stairwell. An inward leaning. A low constant note under the festival noise.
More.

Not Rei's more. A more that belonged to nothing in particular. It did not resolve into wanting food or drink or company. It was simply appetite with the object filed off, reaching into him and trying his own emptiness for a handle.
The man was at a standing counter eating gyoza, and he was already half turned to leave before the plate was finished.

He was in his late thirties and looked older. Tall, spare, all long limbs, his hair grown out and not recently cut. He was neat in a way that had gone threadbare at the cuffs. A jacket with too many pockets. A bag he could pick up in one movement. He had the economy of someone who owned only what he could carry and had learned to eat fast and walk faster.

He did not sit. Rei would come to understand that he had not properly sat down in three years. The stools and benches and chairs of the city were all very slightly his enemies. The one piece of furniture he truly feared was a bed.

He noticed Rei the moment the appetite in the air touched Rei and touched back. He felt his own register find a foothold in a stranger. His eyes went to Rei with the tired, practised wariness of a man who has been hunted by quieter things than this boy.

"You feel it," he said around the last gyoza, already paying, already moving. "Then walk while you talk. If I stand here much longer it learns this counter. I like this counter. I'd rather not have to give it up."
So they walked.

They passed a conveyor-belt sushi bar where the plates went round under a lit counter. A young salaryman sat at the end of it, tie loosened, a tower of empty plates at his elbow. He was reaching for another before he had finished chewing. His face had the slack, absent look of a man who is not eating because he is hungry, but because he cannot think what else to do with his hands.
As Satoru walked past the window, the man's hand stopped halfway to the belt. He blinked. He looked at the plates beside him as if seeing them for the first time, and set his chopsticks down.

"That's it," Satoru said, without looking back. "That's the whole job. The appetite gets into a man and he doesn't know why he's eating. I walk past and take the empty off him, and he goes home and thinks he's had enough. Fifty of those a night. A hundred, in a bad week." He did not slow. "If I'd stopped at the counter beside him, I'd have given it to him instead. The empty goes where the holder is. That's why the holder can't be anywhere for long. He set a pace that was not quite hurried and never once slackened. He threaded through the festival crowds, the families coming back from the temple with their lanterns, the long warm tables of the night markets. As he moved, the more moved with him, half a step behind. A thing on a leash that he kept barely ahead of by never, ever stopping.
"Inoue Satoru," he said, once they were clear of the counter and the appetite had unhooked from it. "Ninth of the Thirteen. I carry Hunger."
He said it the way another man might say he had a bad heart. A fact about the body. Load-bearing, permanent, not up for discussion.
"And before you ask the thing everyone asks. No. I cannot just put it down for one night and sleep. That is exactly the thing I cannot do. That is the whole job."

He explained it as they crossed from Ueno toward Okachimachi, under the railway arches where the late izakaya were still going. He explained it walking, always walking, because explaining it standing still would have been demonstrating the problem.

"A holder doesn't satisfy the register," he said. "You can't. Hunger isn't a wanting that gets a thing and stops. It's the wanting underneath all the wantings. The empty that's there before there's anything to fill it. My job isn't to feed it. My job is to keep it from finding out where it lives."

His jacket pockets bulged. Rei saw what with when Satoru reached into one. Wrapped sweets, rice crackers, a paper twist of roasted chestnuts. He ate the way other men smoked, without noticing, to keep his hands and mouth busy so the rest of him would not slow down.

"Don't look at me like that," Satoru said. "I'm not hungry. I'm never hungry. It isn't my hunger." He offered Rei a chestnut. Rei took it. It was still warm, and it tasted of nothing at all, as if the empty walking beside them had eaten the taste out of it first.
He bought a skewer from a stall without breaking stride, ate it in four bites, and dropped the stick into a bin he had clearly used before.

"Every time I stop somewhere long enough, it learns the place. It writes the address down. And a Hunger seat with a fixed address starts pulling the empty toward it. Out of the people nearby. Out of the food, which stops being enough. Out of the holder, until the holder is the hungriest thing in the room and the room is starting to come apart. So I move. Three years now. The appetite doesn't get a door because I don't have one."

At the next crossing the lights changed against them. Rei stopped at the kerb. Satoru did not. One moment he was beside Rei. The next he was on the far pavement, thirty metres off, waiting, with no gap in between where he had walked. Rei crossed on the green and Satoru fell in beside him as if nothing had happened.

"Teleportation," Satoru said. "Short hops. The seat needs fast hands. Hunger doesn't flare in one place, it flares in fifty little places at once all over the city, and somebody has to be at each of them before it settles." He rubbed his eyes. "I try not to do it in front of people. It feels like cheating at walking."
"Gin's file said you were an emergency succession."

"The man before me died. Three years ago. The seat went empty, and they found me and put me in it in months. It's meant to take years. Years of preparation, years of being taught by the one before you." He shrugged. "I know where the gaps are. I'm managing them. The Axis knows too."

Walking that warm midnight beside a man who could not stop, Rei understood that this was the unglamorous physics of a seat. Not a throne. A sentence. Not power but a load a man arranged his whole life around, so that he never dropped it.

Satoru was exhausted in a way that had become structural. He slept in ninety-minute pieces on moving trains. He had not tasted a meal in years, because eating was maintenance and never pleasure. He had given up every fixed thing a life is built from. A home. A chair he liked. A person who knew which station to find him at. All so that the empty he carried would never learn an address it could pull the world into.

"People think the hard part is the hunger," he said. "It isn't. The hard part is that I'd give anything to stop. Anything. And the one thing the register knows about me, the only handle it's got, is how badly I want to sit down."

And there it was. The crack. The same shape Rei had seen in two other failing seats. The human want that the impersonal register got its fingers into. The fear holder had been afraid of failing. This one was starving for rest.

The domain was weather. Blameless. One of the true empties the world was built on, and someone had to carry it. But the longing to set it down was his. It was exactly the lack the appetite reached for. And he could not stop producing it, because he was a tired man not yet forty who looked fifty and had not slept in a bed since before he could comfortably remember.

He glanced sideways at Rei as they walked, reading the suppressed registers, the searching, the keyed thing. The others had looked at Rei with caution or with hope. Satoru looked at him with something worse. Recognition.
"You've got an empty too," he said quietly. "Walled up. I can feel the door from here. How do you stand it not eating you?"
Rei asked him the question he asked all of them now. He had stopped believing in coincidence and started believing in a method.
"Has anyone been kind to you lately? Soft-voiced. Turned up around the time it got harder. Offered you something that felt like exactly what you needed, and left you a little worse than before."
Satoru stopped.
He actually stopped, for the first time. One full second of stillness that visibly cost him. The appetite lurched forward against its leash, and he made himself move again.

"There's a woman," he said. "Kitagawa-san. Runs a little guesthouse near Nippori. The old wooden kind. She found me. I don't know how. I don't have an address for anyone to find. She said she had a room with my name on it. No charge. A real bed. She said a man my age shouldn't have to sleep standing up. She was so kind about it I nearly cried, and I haven't done that in years."
He swallowed.

"I've been three times. I never stay. But each time it's harder to leave. And each time, for about a week after, the appetite is worse. I thought that was just wanting the bed I couldn't have. The contrast."
It was not the contrast. Rei knew this handwriting now. The patient kindness that hollowed out the chairs holding the sky up.

Someone had found the one thing a Hunger holder could not afford to want. A place to stop. They had wrapped it in a soft voice and a real bed and a room with his name on it. Every time he came, they let him taste the rest he had denied himself for three years. And they let the appetite taste the address he had spent three years refusing to give it.

They were not trying to feed him. They were teaching the empty where its holder would live if he ever let himself. Drawing it toward a fixed door one merciful night at a time. Until the seat found an address, and the ninth domain settled and started to pull. Beside a membrane already thin, in the one week of the year when the doors between here and the other side were propped open for the dead.

"I know what they're after," Satoru said, when Rei told him. He did not sound surprised. He sounded like a man hearing a diagnosis he had been avoiding. "We all feel it in the network. Somebody organised has been leaning on the seats for years. Not loose things. A campaign. It's coordinated from the very top of the scale, the Class S things that have their own institutions on the far side. And mine is the seat they want most." He walked faster. "They've been testing. Twice at the Shibuya crossing, two test events the CVD wrote up as crowd incidents. They keep two contact points in the underground mall at the Ikebukuro west exit. They don't want to take the thirteenth. They want it never to be filled, ever. A vacant thirteenth means the Axis is stretched across two jobs, and a stretched Axis makes mistakes. They've been living off its mistakes for three years. If they get mine as well..."
"Two empty seats," Rei said.

"Two empty seats, and the Axis tries to hold mine too and can't, because it's already holding Duty. Then it all starts sliding." He nodded north, toward Kita. "When Hunger goes, it won't go quietly. It'll go to the old works at Kita-Ōji first. The pre-war factories. There are suffering beings in those buildings nobody ever cleared. Hunger is what wakes them. That's where the first crossings would be."

"She asked me to come tonight," he said, and the appetite spiked with the saying of it, the way the fear had spiked when the stairwell holder named her visitor. "She said the room's made up. She said I looked so tired last time. She's not... I don't think she's pretending. That's the thing. I think she really does want to give a tired man a place to sleep. That's what makes it impossible to say no to."
He was walking faster now, as if he could outpace the offer itself.

"And I want to go. God help me, I want to go and lie down on a real bed and sleep eight hours and let it learn the address and let the whole thing settle and be someone else's problem. Because I am so tired, and three years is so long, and a bed is such a small thing to want."
He looked at Rei.
"So before I walk myself to Nippori like I do every time, tell me what you are. Because I think you might be the only person who could make it so I don't have to."
What Rei did was not the bed and it was not the road.

He had walked enough of the night beside Satoru to see the trap whole. Satoru could not rest, because rest meant stopping, and stopping meant an address, and an address meant the seat would settle and pull. The guesthouse offered him stillness and poisoned it. The street offered him safety and never let him stop. They were the same sentence wearing two faces.
So Rei gave him the third thing, the one nobody had offered in three years. He carried the motion for him.

blocks.cap: The whole city moving through the Obon night

blocks.p: It was Obon, and the whole city was moving. Families were coming home from the graves. Lantern-lit processions wound through the streets. A slow river of people was heading down to the water for the tōrō nagashi, where paper lanterns are set out on the current to carry the dead back to the far shore.

Rei took him down to the river, into the moving crowd. He walked on the outside of Satoru, between him and every place he might stop. He kept the pace so that Satoru did not have to. And for the length of the procession, inside the motion of ten thousand people walking the dead home, a man who had not sat down in three years closed his eyes and let himself be carried.

He did not sleep, exactly. But he rested, in a way he had forgotten was possible. He was moving without driving the movement, held inside a current larger than his own exhaustion. The appetite found no door, because the whole street was in motion and there was no still place for it to write down.

Rei walked and kept walking. He took the empty into his own walled chest, where it could not reach all the way in. He went half a step ahead of Satoru the way he had climbed half a step ahead of the fear. Being hungry in the right place, on purpose, so that the river of the man ran clean for one hour.

It was the worst kind of useful. Rei felt the old quiet voice start up under the festival noise. See, the wall is good, the empty can't eat you, why would you ever take it down. He kept that voice at the edge of the crowd with the rest of what he carried. He walked Satoru down to the water with his eyes closed and his face, for the first time, not braced.
At the river's edge the lanterns were going out onto the black water by the hundred. Small boxes of orange light, loosed downstream toward the dead.
Satoru opened his eyes and watched them go.
"They don't stop either," he said softly. "That's the trick of it. They're not at rest. They're at peace because they're still moving."

Something in him had eased that no bed could have eased. Not the hunger. That was weather and would always be weather. It was the three-year cramp of a man who had believed his only choices were a chair that killed him or a road that never ended.

Rei had not cured the ninth seat. He had shown its holder a way to be still inside motion. That was the one thing the soft-voiced woman's bed could never give him. Her stillness came with an address. Rei's came with a current.
"I didn't know it could be like this," Satoru said, watching the light go downstream. "I thought stopping was the only way to rest. Nobody ever told me I could rest by being carried."

blocks.cap: The old wooden guesthouse near Nippori, its screens lit gold

blocks.p: Kitagawa-san was waiting near the bottom of the guesthouse lane when Rei walked him back up from the river.

blocks.cap: Kitagawa-san at the bottom of the guesthouse lane

blocks.p: She was exactly as he had described her. A small kind woman in late middle age, an apron over a summer yukata. Behind her the guesthouse glowed warm, its paper screens lit gold. Rei did not doubt there was a real bed made up inside with Satoru's name beside it.
She saw that he was not alone. And she saw, the way the soft-voiced ones always saw, that something tonight had not gone the way the method needed.

"Inoue-san," she said. Her voice was truly glad and truly worried, and the worry did its soft work of reaching for the want. "You look so tired. The room's ready. It's always ready. You don't have to keep doing this to yourself."

Rei watched him hear it. The rest. The room. The small mercy that was also a door the appetite would love to learn. And he watched it fail to land the way it had landed three times before. For one hour tonight, Satoru had learned that rest and stopping were not the same thing. A man who has felt the difference cannot quite unfeel it.

She did not push. Her kind never pushed. Pushing would show the method, and the method only worked while it looked like nothing but kindness. She simply took in that tonight's bed would go unslept in. She recalculated with that frictionless ease and folded her hands.
"The room will keep," she said, mild and warm, to him and past him to Rei. "It's no trouble. Everyone needs somewhere to stop, in the end. Even him."

The even him was aimed at Rei. It was small and precise. A note being filed. The ninth seat could be carried through motion by someone with a wall instead of an address. The keyed thing that had walked the river tonight was exactly the kind of tool the work could use. Without meaning to, Rei had shown the other side a tool while he thought he was only saving a man. He had come to keep a holder from his door. He had also taught the people thinning the wall a new way to think about doors. And about him.

When she had gone back inside and the gold light of the screens had closed behind her, Satoru stood in the lane. The festival murmured its way down toward the river. Beyond the rooftops, the lanterns were still going out on the black water.

He was not fixed. He would be moving again before dawn, because the seat was a sentence and Rei had not commuted it. But he stood in the lane like a man who had remembered that there is a difference between a road and a current.
"She'll find another one," he said. "Somebody who hasn't learned the river yet. There's always somebody more tired than they can stand to be."

He was not wrong. Somewhere across the thin ward there was a seat for every want, and a soft voice with a bed or a meal or a kindness shaped exactly to that want. Rei could not walk every river. But he had walked this one.
"Thank you for carrying it," Satoru said.
It was the oddest thanks and the truest. He meant, thank you for showing me I don't only get to choose between starving and stopping.
Then he was gone, between one step and the next, the way he had crossed the road.

Rei walked home alone along the river. Despair, Rage, Fear, and now Hunger. Four seats, he thought, and every one of them visited by someone soft, and all of it in the same fortnight. A campaign that had been patient for years had suddenly begun to hurry. He wondered what it knew about the calendar that he did not.
